title: Actors and reentrancy
summary: An actor is like a class that lets only one caller touch its data at a time, so there are no data races. But while it waits at an `await`, other callers can get in - re-check state after every `await`.
body: **In simple words:** An actor protects its own variables. From outside you must `await` to call it, and the actor runs one request at a time, like a single bank teller serving a queue of customers.
**Real-life analogy:** One bank teller. Customers line up; the teller handles one at a time, so the cash drawer is never messed up by two people at once.

**Reentrancy (the tricky part):** if the teller says "wait, I need to call head office" (an `await`), they serve the next customer meanwhile. When they come back, the drawer may have changed. In code: a method checks state, awaits, then writes - and another call may have run in between.

**Classic bug:** an image cache actor checks `cache[url]`, does not find it, awaits a download, then stores. Two callers asking for the same URL both download. Fix: store the in-flight `Task` in the dictionary before awaiting, so the second caller awaits the same task.

**Actor vs lock:** actors are for async code. For a tiny synchronous critical section (a counter, a dictionary read) called from non-async code, a `Mutex` is simpler and does not force `await` on every caller.
**Cost:** each call into an actor from outside can switch threads ("actor hop"). Batch work into one call instead of many tiny calls in a loop.
keyPoints: Actors serialize access to their state: no data races, compiler-enforced.
Actors are reentrant: other calls can run while one is suspended at `await`.
Re-check invariants after every `await`; store in-flight tasks to dedupe work.
`@MainActor` is a global actor tied to the main thread.
Use `Mutex` for small synchronous critical sections; actors for async shared state.

mistakes: Assuming an actor method runs start to finish without interruption.
Making everything an actor, forcing `await` everywhere and adding hops.
followups: **Why are actors reentrant instead of blocking?** Non-reentrant actors could deadlock when two actors await each other.
**Is an actor Sendable?** Yes, always - it protects its own state.
**Can an actor run on a specific queue?** Yes, with a custom executor, e.g. to wrap a non-thread-safe C library.
